replies.author: liachra
replies.text: I use UAPP (Universal Audio Player Pro). Supports local file playback & streaming through Tidal and/or Qobuz. It also supports streaming from a self hosted DLNA server as well. You can add local playback & Tidal/Qobuz tracks into the same playlists so you don't have to jump between apps/services for different albums/tracks. Only issue is it is proprietary but considering GrapheneOS has storage scopes that isn't a huge issue. I haven't been able to find any open-source music player that will play tracks bit-perfectly with USB DACs so I wouldn't recommend them as all your music will get resampled through Android's crappy audio stack You can either obtain UAPP through Google Play or direct purchase on their website.

replies.author: liachra
replies.text: liachra The DLNA server would probably be easier than running Navidrome as I heard that can be a pain to keep reliable especially on a laptop. You could also look into Roon for a complete solution as it has it's own mobile apps and integrates with high end AVRs and things like that but for the most straight forward way to run at home if you're wanting to "stream" your purchased files would be the DLNA server on your thinkpad with Tailscale (for external/not at home on the go access) and use UAPP on your phone, you'll get the added benefit of optionally streaming Tidal or Qobuz and integrate them into the same playlists as your purchased file also.

replies.author: four
replies.text:
schweizer What makes you think Spotify is a shady company?

I wouldn't say they're more shady than other surveillance capitalism companies, but any surveillance capitalism company is shady as hell.

• They collect everything you do in the app. Searches, skips, interactions. They make inferences about your age, interests, preferences, and scans for other devices on your Wi-Fi.

• They take data from marketing and ad partners and their inferences about you. And Spotify shares your data with those ad partners.

• Personalized ads are enabled by default. If you opt out, you still get ads based on context of what you're listening to.

• Your listen history Is kept for the length of your account.

• Your data including voice recordings, if you use them, can be used to train machine learning models and there's no opt-out.

• They were fined by Sweden's data protection authority in 2023

Is this an inaccurate summary of their privacy practices and history?

replies.author: liachra
replies.text:
schweizer Well first off, excluding YouTube Music they pay the least to their artists out of all the streaming services.

schweizer It is not that buying CDs would support artists more. It is the labels that take a huge share.

This is naive. Yes the labels take a huge share however I personally know many artists who receive a bigger portion of the income with CDs/Vinyl than they do on streaming services.10,000 streams a month equal around 10 cents (if you're lucky), a couple hundred CD & vinyl sales are in the dollars. Additionally not every artist are with a major label and only sell CD's through direct purchase meaning they receive majority of the cost you pay for an album (minus printing & payment/store-front processing fees).

Yes CDs/vinyl sales are smaller than streaming but the artists that have noticed a incline in CD sales are noticing a more of a profit hence why you see so many independent artists are heavily pushing physical media sales to their audience. The more people cop on to this the better for them.

schweizer They do not sell customer data

Completely untrue. They aggregate with many major advertising & marketing platforms

replies.author: dryfter
replies.text:
AKRAKU Everyone has their own use cases and limitations when it comes to music. It's not as cut and dry as "stop subscribing to streaming services and buy the album" for some people.

For myself, I have a problem with self-control. I know this because I lived it at the time when I had 500+ CD's and was still buying numerous ones every month. It's much easier for me to support the artists on a platform that at least pays the most (Qobuz or Deezer) for as cheap as I can since I'm disabled and on a fixed income. Here in the US Deezer is around $12/month. There is ZERO way I'm equaling that buying a CD a month even if I could limit myself. Also, I live in a studio apartment, I have no room for CD's at all. So for my use case streaming is perfect as it allows me to support the artist the only way I can right now while getting a very diverse mix of music that I could not afford to buy. If I somehow end up with a little extra money at the end of the month then I look into merch from an artist, but I generally don't like to be a walking billboard, which is a whole other topic of conversation that probably doesn't belong here.

Also, my music listening world expanded by leaps and bounds when I started using streaming services. Prior to that I limited myself to pretty much metal / rock CD's and occasionally got recommendations from magazines I read that were hit or miss and some regrets.
